screens.title: Connecting React to MetaMask and Ethereum Providers
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you'll learn the exact steps a React dApp uses to connect to a user's Ethereum wallet. We begin by detecting whether a provider like MetaMask is available in the browser. If present, a window. ethereum object appears and becomes our entry point. Next, we'll request permission to access accounts using the standard RPC call, which opens a secure approval dialog in MetaMask. After connection, the app must listen for dynamic events: when a user changes accounts or switches networks, those events fire and your app should update state and reinitialize the Web3 instance as needed. Finally, we will centralize this logic in a React Context so every component can read the Web3 provider, the current account, and the chain ID without prop drilling. This matters because without the provider your app can only read public data; with a proper connection you can sign transactions and call smart contract methods. A simple example is a “Connect Wallet” flow that requests accounts on click, then shows the connected address and chain ID in the UI. Keep an eye out for a common pitfall: many dApps forget to reinitialize Web3 after a chain change, which can lead to sending transactions to the wrong network. As you explore, think about how to make the connection logic reliable and user-friendly.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Connecting React to MetaMask
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

Connect React to MetaMask

Walk through detection, permission requests, event handling, and a Context-based pattern to share Web3 and account state across your app.

Detect Provider
Check for window.ethereum on load; guide users to install MetaMask when absent.
Request Access
Call eth_requestAccounts on a user action and handle success or denial gracefully.
Share via Context
Create a Web3Provider to make web3, account, and chainId available app-wide.
Explore Key Topics
Detect Provider
window.ethereum presence check
Request Accounts
eth_requestAccounts on user action
Context Pattern
Web3Provider and useWeb3 hook
From detection to Context
A short conceptual flow: detect provider → request access → listen for events → expose state via Context for global use.
In this lesson
Make wallet connection reliable and visible.
Coming up
A code walkthrough of a Web3Provider implementation.
Note: This presentation focuses on patterns and code you will implement locally. It avoids external links and focuses on code and UX practices for connecting a React dApp to MetaMask.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Part 1
screens.narratorSegment: First, you will learn how to detect whether MetaMask or another compatible provider is installed in the user's browser. Detection relies on the presence of a window. ethereum object. In practice you check this inside a lifecycle hook, like useEffect on component mount, so the app knows immediately whether a provider is available. Second, you will implement the logic to request user account access. The eth_requestAccounts RPC method triggers MetaMask to display a confirmation dialog to the user. This request should normally happen in response to a clear user action, such as clicking a Connect Wallet control; asking automatically on load creates a poor user experience and may be blocked. A concrete example: your app shows a static “Connect Wallet” panel that, when the user intends to use the dApp, calls eth_requestAccounts. Handle the returned Promise to set state on success and show helpful messaging on error or denial. A common misconception is that detection alone grants access — it does not. Detection only tells you a provider exists; you still need to request permission to access private accounts. These capabilities together let your dApp move from read-only data to transaction-capable workflows.

01 — Detect Provider
Confirm window.ethereum exists. This tells you a compatible wallet is installed.
VERIFIED COMPETENCY MILESTONE
Mnemonic: think of detection as checking for a front door before knocking. If there's no door, guide the user to install the wallet.
02 — Request Accounts

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Part 2
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this chapter you will be able to detect MetaMask, request access, react to wallet events, and provide a shared Web3 instance to your entire React app. Detecting MetaMask means checking for window. ethereum inside a setup hook so your app can immediately present the correct UI path. Requesting accounts uses eth_requestAccounts and should happen after clear user intent; handle both the success case, where you store account addresses in state, and error cases, including the user denying access. You will also implement listeners for accountsChanged and chainChanged so the UI updates when a user switches accounts or networks. Finally, you will wrap your App in a Web3Provider that initializes Web3 with window. ethereum and exposes web3, accounts, chainId, isMetaMaskInstalled, and a connectWallet function. A common misconception is to treat the initial connection as enough—remember that networks and accounts can change at any time. Practice by building the provider and then using the useWeb3 hook in a component to display currentAccount and chainId. That hands-on pattern is what makes real dApps responsive and reliable.

screens.title: What is window.ethereum and why it matters
screens.narratorSegment: The window. ethereum object is the handshake between a web page and an Ethereum wallet extension. It is not part of React or your app — it is injected by MetaMask or another compatible provider into the global browser context. Detecting this object is the app's first signal that it can attempt account-based interactions. Concretely, when window. ethereum exists you can request RPC methods like eth_accounts, eth_chainId, and eth_requestAccounts. Use an effect that runs on mount to check for window. ethereum so the app can present the correct UI path immediately. A practical example: when your app loads, check window. ethereum; if it is undefined, display an install prompt or an informational message explaining how to get a compatible wallet. A common misconception is that presence implies permission. It does not. The provider being present means the wallet interface exists, but you still need to call the appropriate RPC to obtain account addresses. Another subtle point is that some browsers may block or delay injection until the extension initializes; the check should be tolerant and re-run when appropriate. Key takeaway: detecting window. ethereum enables richer interactions, but detection alone does not grant access to user accounts — request permission explicitly.

keyIdea.title: Provider definition
keyIdea.text: window.ethereum is the injected provider object that exposes RPC methods for account and network interactions.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › What is window.ethereum
Claim

window.ethereum is an injected provider object from MetaMask that exposes methods your dApp uses to read accounts and send RPC requests to the wallet.

Concrete example
// Check provider in useEffect if (window.ethereum) { // provider exists — show connect option } else { // prompt user to install MetaMask }
Common misconception

Presence of window.ethereum does not mean your dApp has account access. You must call eth_requestAccounts to obtain permission to view or use accounts.

Why this matters

Detecting window.ethereum determines whether your dApp can move beyond public reads and start requesting user signatures and transactions. If you skip this step you cannot prompt for account access, and your app stays read-only.

Quick checks
  • Open console and type window.ethereum — should not be undefined when MetaMask is installed.
  • Use eth_accounts to check whether any accounts are currently connected without prompting the user.
Key Takeaway

Detect window.ethereum on load, but always request accounts before attempting account-based actions.

screens.title: Requesting Account Access (eth_requestAccounts)
screens.narratorSegment: Requesting account access is a deliberate, user-driven step. The key RPC call is eth_requestAccounts invoked through window. ethereum. request. It returns a Promise that resolves to an array of account addresses when approved or rejects if the user denies the request or an error occurs. Because this opens a wallet confirmation dialog, it should be initiated by a clear user action, for example, a Connect Wallet control or an explicit settings flow. On success, store the returned accounts in your React state and set the currentAccount to accounts[0]. On error, show a helpful message and avoid repeatedly prompting the user. A concrete pattern is: check if window. ethereum exists, then present a static connect affordance; when the user triggers connect, call eth_requestAccounts and set state on resolution. Be careful not to treat eth_requestAccounts as a silent read — browsers expect it to be user-initiated. A common mistake is calling eth_requestAccounts on page load; this creates a poor UX and can be blocked. Example handling includes try/catch around the await call, logging the error, and showing a user-friendly notice if permission was denied. The takeaway: request responsibly, handle both outcomes, and keep the user informed.

keyIdea.title: Account request pattern
keyIdea.text: Call eth_requestAccounts in response to user intent; handle the returned account array or permission denial gracefully.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Request Accounts
Process: Request flow
  1. Check for window.ethereum.
  2. Present an explicit Connect Wallet control to the user.
  3. On user action call window.ethereum.request({ method: 'eth_requestAccounts' }).
  4. On success set accounts in state. On error show a helpful message.
Example handling
async function connectWallet() {
  if (!window.ethereum) return; // prompt install
  try {
    const accounts = await window.ethereum.request({ method: 'eth_requestAccounts' });
    setAccounts(accounts);
  } catch (err) {
    // user denied or other error
    console.error('Error connecting to MetaMask:', err);
  }
}
Common mistake
Triggering eth_requestAccounts automatically on page load. This should be user-initiated to respect browser behavior and user expectation.
Concrete scenario

User clicks Connect Wallet. The call opens MetaMask. If the user approves, your app receives an array like ['0xabc...'] and you display the connected account. If they deny, show a retry or instructions.

Check your UX
  • Avoid repeated prompts after denial.
  • Display clear success and error messages.
  • Keep connect logic in one place so it is easy to test.
Key Takeaway

Request accounts only after explicit user intent, handle both success and denial, and update state without reloading the page.

screens.title: Listening for accountsChanged and chainChanged
screens.narratorSegment: Once a wallet is connected, the user can change their selected account or switch networks at any time. MetaMask exposes two events to detect these changes: accountsChanged and chainChanged. Subscribing to these events allows your app to update its state and, when necessary, reinitialize the Web3 instance. For accountsChanged, the handler receives a new accounts array; update accounts state and set currentAccount to the first entry or clear state if the array is empty. For chainChanged, update your chainId state and recreate the Web3 instance so subsequent calls target the correct network. A concrete example: attach window. ethereum. on('accountsChanged', handler) inside a setup effect after verifying window. ethereum exists. Equally important is cleanup: when the component unmounts remove the listeners to avoid memory leaks. A common misconception is that changing the selected account only affects UI; in practice it affects transaction signing and data queries tied to the account. Another pitfall is neglecting to reinitialize Web3 after a chain change, which can lead to interacting with the wrong network. The takeaway: subscribe and update reactively, and always clean up event listeners in your effect's return function.

keyIdea.title: Reactive updates
keyIdea.text: Listen for accountsChanged and chainChanged to update account and chain state and reinitialize Web3 as needed.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Handle Wallet Events
Event: accountsChanged

Fires when the user selects a different account or disconnects. Handler receives an array of accounts.

window.ethereum.on('accountsChanged', (newAccounts) => {
  setAccounts(newAccounts);
  if (newAccounts.length === 0) {
    setWeb3(null); // user disconnected
  } else {
    setWeb3(new Web3(window.ethereum));
  }
});
Event: chainChanged

Fires when the user switches networks. Update chainId and reinitialize Web3 so requests target the correct blockchain.

window.ethereum.on('chainChanged', (newChainId) => {
  setChainId(newChainId);
  setWeb3(new Web3(window.ethereum));
});
Misconception
Assuming account and chain never change during a session. They do, so update UI and provider state accordingly.
Pro tip
Recreate the Web3 instance after chainChanged so your provider points to the new network IDs and RPC endpoints tied to the wallet.
Check your cleanup
Remove listeners on unmount: if window.ethereum.removeListener exists, unregister accountsChanged and chainChanged to prevent duplicate handlers.

screens.title: Web3Provider: centralizing connection logic
screens.narratorSegment: Centralizing connection logic in a Web3Provider simplifies your app and prevents duplicated listeners and state. The provider handles detection, optional existing-account checks, the connectWallet function calling eth_requestAccounts, and subscriptions to accountsChanged and chainChanged. It stores web3, accounts, chainId, and flags like isMetaMaskInstalled and isLoading in local state, then exposes those values through contextValue to any consumer. A concrete implementation pattern uses createContext and a Web3Provider component that returns Web3Context. Provider with the contextValue. Consumers call useWeb3 to access web3, currentAccount, and connectWallet. Important design notes: call eth_accounts on load to see if the user is already connected without prompting; set isLoading while the provider initializes; add cleanup logic to remove listeners when the provider unmounts. A common misconception is that every component should initialize its own Web3; that causes duplicated connections, multiple listeners, and inconsistent state. Instead centralize initialization and re-use the single Web3 instance or reinitialize it only when chainId changes. The key takeaway: Web3Provider produces a single source of truth for wallet connection state across your React tree. Web3Provider: centralizing connection logic means web3provider centralizes detection, connection, event listeners, and exposes a consistent context value for the app.. In practical terms, design a provider component that initializes web3 and exposes connection state.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Web3Provider centralizes detection, connection, event listeners, and exposes a consistent context value for the app.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Web3Provider Architecture
Context value
Provide an object containing web3, accounts, chainId, isMetaMaskInstalled, isLoading, connectWallet, and currentAccount so consumers can read and act on connection state without prop drilling.
Why centralize?
  • Single place to initialize web3 and attach listeners.
  • Avoid repeated Web3 instances and duplicated event handlers.
  • Test and maintain connection logic in one component.
Example shape
const contextValue = { web3, accounts, chainId, isMetaMaskInstalled, isLoading, connectWallet, currentAccount: accounts.length > 0 ? accounts[0] : null, };
Key Takeaway

Keep a single provider component to manage detection, connection, and events so all components share a reliable web3 state.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Web3Provider Code
Core snippet
import React, { createContext, useContext, useState, useEffect, useCallback } from 'react';
import Web3 from 'web3';

const Web3Context = createContext(null);

export const Web3Provider = ({ children }) => {
  const [web3, setWeb3] = useState(null);
  const [accounts, setAccounts] = useState([]);
  const [chainId, setChainId] = useState(null);
  const [isMetaMaskInstalled, setIsMetaMaskInstalled] = useState(false);
  const [isLoading, setIsLoading] = useState(true);

  const connectWallet = useCallback(async () => {
    if (window.ethereum) {
      try {
        const accounts = await window.ethereum.request({ method: 'eth_requestAccounts' });
        setAccounts(accounts);
        const chainId = await window.ethereum.request({ method: 'eth_chainId' });
        setChainId(chainId);
        setWeb3(new Web3(window.ethereum));
      } catch (error) {
        console.error('Error connecting to MetaMask:', error);
      }
    } else {
      alert('MetaMask is not installed.');
    }
  }, []);

  useEffect(() => {
    // initialization code omitted for brevity in the UI
  }, [connectWallet]);

  return (
    <Web3Context.Provider value={{ web3, accounts, chainId, isMetaMaskInstalled, isLoading, connectWallet, currentAccount: accounts.length > 0 ? accounts[0] : null }}>
      {children}
    </Web3Context.Provider>
  );
};

Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Wrap App & Use Hook
main.jsx example
import React from 'react'
import ReactDOM from 'react-dom/client'
import App from './App.jsx'
import { Web3Provider } from './contexts/Web3Provider.jsx'

ReactDOM.createRoot(document.getElementById('root')).render(
  <React.StrictMode>
    <Web3Provider>
      <App />
    </Web3Provider>
  </React.StrictMode>
)
App.jsx usage
function App() {
  const { isLoading, isMetaMaskInstalled, currentAccount, chainId, connectWallet } = useWeb3();

  if (isLoading) return <div>Loading Web3...</div>

  return (
    <div>
      {!isMetaMaskInstalled && <div>MetaMask not installed</div>}
      {isMetaMaskInstalled && !currentAccount && <div className="connect-pill">Connect Wallet (call connectWallet)</div>}
      {currentAccount && <div>Connected: <code>{currentAccount}</code> Chain: <code>{chainId}</code></div>}
    </div>
  );
}
Key Takeaway

Place Web3Provider at the app root and read connection state via useWeb3 so the app reacts to connect, disconnect, and network changes consistently.

screens.title: eth_accounts vs eth_requestAccounts
screens.narratorSegment: Two similar-looking RPC methods serve different purposes. eth_accounts returns an array of accounts that are already connected to your origin — it does not prompt the user. Use it to check whether the user previously granted access. eth_requestAccounts, by contrast, opens a permission dialog asking the user to approve account access, and therefore must be user-initiated. A practical pattern is to call eth_accounts during initialization to decide whether to show a Connect Wallet control or the connected state immediately. If eth_accounts returns an empty array, display a clear Connect Wallet option and only call eth_requestAccounts when the user triggers it. A common misconception is to call eth_requestAccounts on page load expecting silent behavior; browsers and wallets may block or produce poor UX. Example: in the provider's init function, call window. ethereum. request({ method: 'eth_accounts' }) and, if accounts exist, set web3 and account state. If not, wait for a user action before calling eth_requestAccounts. The takeaway: use eth_accounts for non-intrusive checks and eth_requestAccounts for explicit permission requests. eth_accounts vs eth_requestAccounts means use eth_accounts to check existing connections; use eth_requestaccounts to request permission and open metamask's confirmation dialog.. In practical terms, when to check existing connections and when to prompt the user.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › eth_accounts vs eth_requestAccounts
eth_accounts
Non-intrusive. Returns currently-connected accounts without prompting. Good for initialization checks to see if a user previously granted access.
const accounts = await window.ethereum.request({ method: 'eth_accounts' });
eth_requestAccounts
Prompting. Opens MetaMask to request account access. Should be called on user action to avoid unwanted prompts.
const accounts = await window.ethereum.request({ method: 'eth_requestAccounts' });
Best practice
Call eth_accounts on load; only call eth_requestAccounts after an explicit user action such as clicking Connect Wallet.
Misconception
Do not expect eth_requestAccounts to be silent or suitable for silent checks; it prompts the user and should be used sparingly.

Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Implement Wallet Connection
Steps

Starter snippet
// Inside Web3Provider's useEffect
const accounts = await window.ethereum.request({ method: 'eth_accounts' });
if (accounts.length > 0) { setAccounts(accounts); setWeb3(new Web3(window.ethereum)); }

window.ethereum.on('accountsChanged', handler);
window.ethereum.on('chainChanged', handler);

// Cleanup:
if (window.ethereum.removeListener) {
  window.ethereum.removeListener('accountsChanged', () => {});

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you'll learn the exact steps a React dApp uses to connect to a user's Ethereum wallet. We begin by detecting whether a provider like MetaMask is available in the browser. If present, a window. ethereum object appears and becomes our entry point. Next, we'll request permission to access accounts using the standard RPC call, which opens a secure approval dialog in MetaMask. After connection, the app must listen for dynamic events: when a user changes accounts or switches networks, those events fire and your app should update state and reinitialize the Web3 instance as needed. Finally, we will centralize this logic in a React Context so every component can read the Web3 provider, the current account, and the chain ID without prop drilling. This matters because without the provider your app can only read public data; with a proper connection you can sign transactions and call smart contract methods. A simple example is a “Connect Wallet” flow that requests accounts on click, then shows the connected address and chain ID in the UI. Keep an eye out for a common pitfall: many dApps forget to reinitialize Web3 after a chain change, which can lead to sending transactions to the wrong network. As you explore, think about how to make the connection logic reliable and user-friendly.

First, you will learn how to detect whether MetaMask or another compatible provider is installed in the user's browser. Detection relies on the presence of a window. ethereum object. In practice you check this inside a lifecycle hook, like useEffect on component mount, so the app knows immediately whether a provider is available. Second, you will implement the logic to request user account access. The eth_requestAccounts RPC method triggers MetaMask to display a confirmation dialog to the user. This request should normally happen in response to a clear user action, such as clicking a Connect Wallet control; asking automatically on load creates a poor user experience and may be blocked. A concrete example: your app shows a static “Connect Wallet” panel that, when the user intends to use the dApp, calls eth_requestAccounts. Handle the returned Promise to set state on success and show helpful messaging on error or denial. A common misconception is that detection alone grants access — it does not. Detection only tells you a provider exists; you still need to request permission to access private accounts. These capabilities together let your dApp move from read-only data to transaction-capable workflows.

By the end of this chapter you will be able to detect MetaMask, request access, react to wallet events, and provide a shared Web3 instance to your entire React app. Detecting MetaMask means checking for window. ethereum inside a setup hook so your app can immediately present the correct UI path. Requesting accounts uses eth_requestAccounts and should happen after clear user intent; handle both the success case, where you store account addresses in state, and error cases, including the user denying access. You will also implement listeners for accountsChanged and chainChanged so the UI updates when a user switches accounts or networks. Finally, you will wrap your App in a Web3Provider that initializes Web3 with window. ethereum and exposes web3, accounts, chainId, isMetaMaskInstalled, and a connectWallet function. A common misconception is to treat the initial connection as enough—remember that networks and accounts can change at any time. Practice by building the provider and then using the useWeb3 hook in a component to display currentAccount and chainId. That hands-on pattern is what makes real dApps responsive and reliable.

The window. ethereum object is the handshake between a web page and an Ethereum wallet extension. It is not part of React or your app — it is injected by MetaMask or another compatible provider into the global browser context. Detecting this object is the app's first signal that it can attempt account-based interactions. Concretely, when window. ethereum exists you can request RPC methods like eth_accounts, eth_chainId, and eth_requestAccounts. Use an effect that runs on mount to check for window. ethereum so the app can present the correct UI path immediately. A practical example: when your app loads, check window. ethereum; if it is undefined, display an install prompt or an informational message explaining how to get a compatible wallet. A common misconception is that presence implies permission. It does not. The provider being present means the wallet interface exists, but you still need to call the appropriate RPC to obtain account addresses. Another subtle point is that some browsers may block or delay injection until the extension initializes; the check should be tolerant and re-run when appropriate. Key takeaway: detecting window. ethereum enables richer interactions, but detection alone does not grant access to user accounts — request permission explicitly.

Requesting account access is a deliberate, user-driven step. The key RPC call is eth_requestAccounts invoked through window. ethereum. request. It returns a Promise that resolves to an array of account addresses when approved or rejects if the user denies the request or an error occurs. Because this opens a wallet confirmation dialog, it should be initiated by a clear user action, for example, a Connect Wallet control or an explicit settings flow. On success, store the returned accounts in your React state and set the currentAccount to accounts[0]. On error, show a helpful message and avoid repeatedly prompting the user. A concrete pattern is: check if window. ethereum exists, then present a static connect affordance; when the user triggers connect, call eth_requestAccounts and set state on resolution. Be careful not to treat eth_requestAccounts as a silent read — browsers expect it to be user-initiated. A common mistake is calling eth_requestAccounts on page load; this creates a poor UX and can be blocked. Example handling includes try/catch around the await call, logging the error, and showing a user-friendly notice if permission was denied. The takeaway: request responsibly, handle both outcomes, and keep the user informed.

Once a wallet is connected, the user can change their selected account or switch networks at any time. MetaMask exposes two events to detect these changes: accountsChanged and chainChanged. Subscribing to these events allows your app to update its state and, when necessary, reinitialize the Web3 instance. For accountsChanged, the handler receives a new accounts array; update accounts state and set currentAccount to the first entry or clear state if the array is empty. For chainChanged, update your chainId state and recreate the Web3 instance so subsequent calls target the correct network. A concrete example: attach window. ethereum. on('accountsChanged', handler) inside a setup effect after verifying window. ethereum exists. Equally important is cleanup: when the component unmounts remove the listeners to avoid memory leaks. A common misconception is that changing the selected account only affects UI; in practice it affects transaction signing and data queries tied to the account. Another pitfall is neglecting to reinitialize Web3 after a chain change, which can lead to interacting with the wrong network. The takeaway: subscribe and update reactively, and always clean up event listeners in your effect's return function.

Centralizing connection logic in a Web3Provider simplifies your app and prevents duplicated listeners and state. The provider handles detection, optional existing-account checks, the connectWallet function calling eth_requestAccounts, and subscriptions to accountsChanged and chainChanged. It stores web3, accounts, chainId, and flags like isMetaMaskInstalled and isLoading in local state, then exposes those values through contextValue to any consumer. A concrete implementation pattern uses createContext and a Web3Provider component that returns Web3Context. Provider with the contextValue. Consumers call useWeb3 to access web3, currentAccount, and connectWallet. Important design notes: call eth_accounts on load to see if the user is already connected without prompting; set isLoading while the provider initializes; add cleanup logic to remove listeners when the provider unmounts. A common misconception is that every component should initialize its own Web3; that causes duplicated connections, multiple listeners, and inconsistent state. Instead centralize initialization and re-use the single Web3 instance or reinitialize it only when chainId changes. The key takeaway: Web3Provider produces a single source of truth for wallet connection state across your React tree. Web3Provider: centralizing connection logic means web3provider centralizes detection, connection, event listeners, and exposes a consistent context value for the app.. In practical terms, design a provider component that initializes web3 and exposes connection state.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.
